heredity-environment-s2.title: Phenylketonuria (PKU): an inherited condition shaped by diet
heredity-environment-s2.html:
Introduction

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inherited condition in which the body cannot break down phenylalanine, a building block of protein found in many foods. Untreated, it builds up and damages the developing brain, causing severe intellectual disability.

Participants

Bickel and colleagues treated a 2-year-old girl in England who had PKU and severe developmental delays.

Method

The researchers gave her a special diet very low in phenylalanine and recorded her behavior and blood levels over several months.

Results

On the diet, her blood levels fell and her alertness and behavior improved; when phenylalanine was added back to her food, her symptoms worsened again.

Discussion

Later work showed that starting the diet in the first weeks of life largely prevents the brain damage, so newborns in many countries are now screened for PKU.

neural-firing-s2.title: Two pain medications and time to relief
neural-firing-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers wanted to know whether a drug that acts like the body's endorphins relieves pain faster than one that does not act on endorphin receptors.

Participants

90 adults having a tooth removed at a dental clinic volunteered. Each was randomly assigned to one of three groups of 30.

Method

After surgery, one group took Drug E, which binds to and activates endorphin receptors; one took Drug N, which reduces swelling but does not act on those receptors; one took a placebo pill. Patients and the dentists who recorded their answers did not know which pill was which. Each patient rated pain from 0 (none) to 10 (worst) every 10 minutes, and relief was the number of minutes until the rating fell below 4.

Results

Average minutes to relief: Drug E 20, Drug N 35, placebo 55. In a follow-up, patients who took Drug E every day for two weeks needed a larger dose to get the same relief.

Invented study for practice.

brain-s2.title: Speech after damage to one brain region
brain-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether damage to the lower part of the left frontal lobe affects producing speech more than understanding it.

Participants

Two groups of adults at one rehabilitation hospital: 10 patients who had a stroke that damaged the lower left frontal lobe (confirmed by brain scans) and 10 patients of similar age whose strokes damaged other areas. A hospital review board approved the study, and every patient (or a family member, when a patient could not sign) gave informed consent. Names were replaced with code numbers in the records.

Method

Each patient described a picture for one minute; speech was scored as the number of words spoken in that minute. Understanding was scored as the number of 20 spoken instructions ("Point to the cup") carried out correctly.

Results

Frontal-damage group: 18 words per minute and 17 of 20 instructions. Other-damage group: 92 words per minute and 18 of 20 instructions.

Invented study for practice.

brain-s3.title: Split-brain patients
brain-s3.html:
Introduction

In the 1960s a small number of people with severe epilepsy that drugs could not control had their corpus callosum cut to stop seizures spreading from one hemisphere to the other. Researchers tested what each hemisphere could do on its own.

Participants

A few adult patients who had this surgery for medical reasons, studied individually (a set of case studies).

Method

Each patient stared at a dot in the middle of a screen while a word or picture was flashed for a fraction of a second to the left or right of the dot. A flash to the right of the dot reaches only the left hemisphere; a flash to the left reaches only the right hemisphere. Patients said what they saw and reached under a screen to find objects by touch.

Results

When a picture was flashed on the right, patients named it easily. When it was flashed on the left, they usually said they saw nothing, yet their left hand could pick out the matching object by touch.

sleep-s1.title: Sleep stages across one night (a hypnogram)
sleep-s1.html: A sleep lab recorded one 17-year-old volunteer's brain waves, eye movements and muscle activity through an 8-hour night (invented data for practice). The graph shows which stage she was in at each moment, from Awake at the top to N3 at the bottom; N1, N2 and N3 are the NREM stages from light to deep. The five REM periods lasted 10, 20, 25, 25, 30 minutes, in order.

sleep-s2.title: Phones at bedtime and teens' sleep
sleep-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether teens who use a phone more in the hour before bed sleep less.

Participants

240 students aged 14 to 18 at three public high schools in one city volunteered. Parents gave permission, students agreed to take part, and answers were stored without names.

Method

For two weeks, each student's phone app recorded minutes of screen use in the hour before the student's bedtime, and a wrist tracker recorded total minutes of sleep each night. The researchers averaged each student's nights.

Results

Students with more screen minutes before bed slept fewer minutes. The correlation was r=−0.42r = -0.42.

Discussion

The authors note that bright screens can delay the evening rise in melatonin, but that the study cannot show the phones caused the shorter sleep.

Invented study for practice.

sensation-s3.title: Who are supertasters?
sensation-s3.html:
Introduction

Researchers had found that a bitter chemical, PROP, tastes strongly bitter to some people and nearly tasteless to others. They asked whether people who taste it strongly differ in their tongues.

Participants

Adult volunteers recruited at a US university.

Method

Participants rated the bitterness of PROP on a scale. The researchers stained the front of each person's tongue with blue food coloring and counted the small bumps that hold taste buds in a standard circle.

Results

People who rated PROP as intensely bitter (supertasters) had many more taste-bud bumps than people who barely tasted it. Women were more often supertasters than men.

items.q: What does <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>0.42</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = -0.42</annotation></semantics></math> tell you about these students?
options: More bedtime screen use went with less sleep, a moderate relationship
More bedtime screen use went with more sleep, a moderate relationship
Bedtime screen use caused 42% less sleep in these students
Screen use and sleep were unrelated in these students

items.q: Which is a third variable that could explain the correlation without phones causing shorter sleep?
options: Heavy homework loads, which keep students up late and on their phones
The wrist tracker, which measured how many minutes each student slept
The number of students, 240, who took part in the study
The two-week length of the study, which covered weekends

items.q: State the operational definition of sleep in this study.

specific.frame: Sleep was measured as ___, recorded by ___.
specific.model: Sleep was operationally defined as the total minutes of sleep each night, recorded by a wrist tracker and averaged over two weeks.

opdef.label: Measure
options: total minutes of sleep each night
how rested each student felt
minutes of screen use before bed

why.1: Feeling rested was never measured; a feeling is not a measure unless the study says how it was scored.
why.2: Screen minutes is the other variable, not sleep.

method.label: Recorded by
options: a wrist tracker
a sleep diary
a phone app

why.1: The summary says a tracker recorded sleep; no diary was used.
why.2: The phone app recorded screen use, not sleep.

items.q: Kenji flies from Los Angeles to Tokyo. For several days he is wide awake at 3 a.m. and sleepy at noon. What best explains this?
options: His circadian rhythm is still set to Los Angeles time
He is spending too long in N3 sleep each night
He has developed narcolepsy from the long flight
His REM sleep has been replaced by NREM sleep

items.q: As she drifts off, Priya suddenly feels as if she is falling and her leg jerks, waking her. In which stage did this most likely happen?
options: N1
N3
REM
N2

items.q: A sleep technician sees a sleeper's EEG show fast, irregular waves like those of waking, while the eyes dart under the lids and the arm and leg muscles are limp. Which stage is this?
options: REM sleep
N3 sleep
N1 sleep
Awake

items.q: A 9-year-old gets up about an hour after falling asleep, walks to the kitchen with open eyes, and remembers nothing in the morning. Which disorder fits, and in which stage does it usually happen?
options: Somnambulism, in N3 sleep
Somnambulism, in REM sleep
Narcolepsy, in REM sleep
REM sleep behavior disorder, in N3 sleep

items.q: A 68-year-old man punches and kicks in his sleep. When woken he describes a dream of fighting off an attacker. Which disorder fits best?
options: REM sleep behavior disorder
Somnambulism
Sleep apnea
Insomnia

items.q: Marcus snores loudly. His partner notices he stops breathing for several seconds, then gasps, many times a night. He is exhausted every day. Which disorder is most likely?
options: Sleep apnea
Narcolepsy
Insomnia
REM sleep behavior disorder

items.q: During a funny conversation, a college student suddenly falls asleep in her chair, and a sleep study shows she enters REM within minutes. Which disorder fits?
options: Narcolepsy
Sleep apnea
Somnambulism
Insomnia

items.q: Which statement matches the activation-synthesis theory of dreaming?
options: In REM, random brainstem signals are woven by the cortex into a story
Dreams replay the day so the brain can sort and store new memories
Sleep lets the body repair tissue and restore energy used during the day
Dreams show hidden wishes that the dreamer would reject while awake

items.q: Students learn a list of word pairs at 9 p.m. Half sleep normally; half are kept awake all night and nap the next afternoon. The next evening, the sleep group recalls more pairs. Which idea does this support?
options: Sleep helps consolidate new memories
Sleep mainly restores the body's energy
Dreams come from random brainstem activity
Sleep timing is set by the circadian rhythm

items.q: For three months, Ana has lain awake for over an hour most nights and wakes at 4 a.m., unable to fall back asleep, and is tired at work. Which disorder fits?
options: Insomnia
Narcolepsy
Sleep apnea
Somnambulism

items.q: To read the small print on a medicine label, Ines looks straight at it. Where in the eye does the image of the print fall, and why does that help?
options: On the fovea, where cones are packed for fine detail
On the blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves the eye
On the lens, which detects color and fine detail
On the outer edge of the retina, where rods are densest

items.q: Out stargazing, Theo notices a faint star is easier to see when he looks slightly to one side of it. What explains this?
options: Off to the side, the image falls where rods are dense; rods work in dim light
Off to the side, the image falls on the fovea, which is packed with cones
Looking away moves the image onto the blind spot, which boosts faint light
Looking away lets the lens collect more light from the faint, distant star

items.q: In the figure, why is there a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the eye?
options: There are no rods or cones there to detect light
The cones there detect color but not any shapes
The lens does not bend light toward that spot
Too many rods there overload the optic nerve

items.q: Light reaching the retina is changed into neural signals that travel along the optic nerve. What is this change called?
options: Transduction
Sensory adaptation
Sensory interaction
Signal detection

items.q: Which statement best describes the two listeners' results?
options: A had more hits and more false alarms; B had fewer of both
A had more hits and also fewer false alarms than B did
B had more hits and also more false alarms than A did
The two listeners gave about the same responses overall

items.q: Which concept best explains why the listeners responded differently to the same sounds?
options: Signal detection theory: rewards and costs shifted how readily each said "tone"
Sensory adaptation: Listener B had grown used to the static and stopped hearing it
Weber's law: the tone was below each listener's just-noticeable difference
Transduction: Listener A's ears turned sound into neural signals faster

items.q: What percent of the tone trials did Listener A detect (her hit rate)?

mistakes.why: 46% divides by all 100 trials. A hit rate is out of the 50 trials that had a tone.
36% is her false-alarm rate. Hits are the tone trials where she said "tone": 46 of 50.

items.q: A radiologist knows that missing a tumor could cost a patient's life. Like Listener A, she tends to report possible tumors readily. What trade-off should she expect?
options: More hits, but also more false alarms
Fewer hits, but also fewer false alarms
More hits and fewer false alarms
No change in hits or false alarms

items.q: Based on the study, which person is most likely a supertaster?
options: Mia, who finds black coffee and raw broccoli unpleasantly bitter
Leo, who adds extra hot sauce because mild food tastes bland
Ava, who stops noticing the smell of coffee after an hour in the kitchen
Sam, who sees colors when he hears music

items.q: Why can this study not show that having more taste buds causes stronger bitter taste?
options: Both variables were measured; neither was manipulated
Food coloring could have changed how PROP tasted
The participants were adults, not children or teens
Bitterness was rated by people, not by a machine

items.q: Besides sweet, salty, sour and bitter, which taste do researchers now recognize for the savory flavor of broth and parmesan?
options: Umami
Oleogustus
Gustation
Olfaction

items.q: Holding a 100-gram letter, Dani can just tell when 2 grams are added. By Weber's law, about how much must be added to a 400-gram package for her to just notice a change?
options: About 8 grams
About 2 grams
About 4 grams
About 20 grams

items.q: A singer can just notice a change of 3 hertz in a 300-hertz tone. Assuming Weber's law holds, what is the smallest change in hertz she would notice in a 900-hertz tone?

mistakes.why: 3 Hz is the change for the 300 Hz tone. By Weber's law the change grows in proportion: 3 / 300 is 1%, and 1% of 900 is 9.
903 is the new tone's pitch, not the size of the change. The just-noticeable change is 1% of 900, which is 9 Hz.

items.q: Owen jumps into a cold lake and gasps, but after five minutes the water feels fine. Which concept explains the change?
options: Sensory adaptation
Transduction
The absolute threshold
Synesthesia

items.q: With a bad cold and a blocked nose, Lucas says his favorite soup tastes like "hot water." Which concept explains this?
options: Sensory interaction
Sensory adaptation
Weber's law
Signal detection theory

items.q: Stare at a green square for 30 seconds, then look at a white wall, and you briefly see a red square. Which theory explains this best?
options: Opponent-process theory
Trichromatic theory
Place theory

items.q: Zach cannot tell the red and green lights on a traffic signal apart by color; he uses their position. Which explanation fits best?

Prosopagnosia
Sensory adaptation
The blind spot
